claim: Many species of animals exhibit an intuitive sense of number.
source: Many species of animals exhibit an intuitive sense of number, suggesting a fundamental neural mechanism for representing numerosity in a visual scene.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge about animal cognition.

claim: An intuitive sense of number suggests a fundamental neural mechanism for representing numerosity in a visual scene.
source: Many species of animals exhibit an intuitive sense of number, suggesting a fundamental neural mechanism for representing numerosity in a visual scene.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of number sense across species.

claim: Early feedforward visual responses are sensitive to numerosity of a dot array.
source: Recent empirical studies demonstrate that early feedforward visual responses are sensitive to numerosity of a dot array but substantially less so to continuous dimensions orthogonal to numerosity, such as size and spacing of the dots.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Early feedforward visual responses are substantially less sensitive to continuous dimensions orthogonal to numerosity, such as size and spacing of the dots.
source: Recent empirical studies demonstrate that early feedforward visual responses are sensitive to numerosity of a dot array but substantially less so to continuous dimensions orthogonal to numerosity, such as size and spacing of the dots.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The mechanisms that extract numerosity are unknown.
source: However, the mechanisms that extract numerosity are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Center-surround contrast filters at different spatial scales with divisive normalization across network units eliminate sensitivity to size and spacing.
source: In an untrained computational model, these principles eliminated sensitivity to size and spacing, making numerosity the main determinant of the neuronal response magnitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Center-surround contrast filters at different spatial scales with divisive normalization make numerosity the main determinant of the neuronal response magnitude.
source: In an untrained computational model, these principles eliminated sensitivity to size and spacing, making numerosity the main determinant of the neuronal response magnitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: A model implementation of center-surround filters and divisive normalization explained both well-known and relatively novel illusions of numerosity perception across space and time.
source: Moreover, a model implementation of these principles explained both well-known and relatively novel illusions of numerosity perception across space and time.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The neural structures and feedforward processes that encode numerosity naturally produce visual illusions of numerosity.
source: This supports the conclusion that the neural structures and feedforward processes that encode numerosity naturally produce visual illusions of numerosity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Humans have an intuitive sense of number that allows numerosity estimation without counting.
source: Humans have an intuitive sense of number that allows numerosity estimation without counting (Dehaene, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dehaene, 2011.

claim: The prevalence of number sense across phylogeny and ontogeny suggests common neural mechanisms that allow the extraction of numerosity information from a visual scene.
source: The prevalence of number sense across phylogeny and ontogeny (Feigenson et al., 2004) suggests common neural mechanisms that allow the extraction of numerosity information from a visual scene.
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Feigenson et al., 2004.

claim: Earlier empirical work highlighted the parietal cortex for numerosity representation.
source: While earlier empirical work highlighted the parietal cortex for numerosity representation (Nieder, 2016), growing evidence suggests that numerosity is processed at a much earlier stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nieder, 2016.

claim: Growing evidence suggests that numerosity is processed at a much earlier stage than the parietal cortex.
source: While earlier empirical work highlighted the parietal cortex for numerosity representation (Nieder, 2016), growing evidence suggests that numerosity is processed at a much earlier stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to subsequent studies.

claim: Early visual cortical activity is uniquely sensitive to the number of a dot array in the absence of any behavioral response.
source: A recent study, using high-temporal resolution electroencephalography together with a novel stimulus design, demonstrated that early visual cortical activity is uniquely sensitive to the number (abbreviated as N) of a dot array in the absence of any behavioral response, but much less so to nonnumerical dimensions that are orthogonal to number (i.e., size and spacing, abbreviated as Sz and Sp, respectively; see Figure 1A; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2016.

claim: Early visual cortical activity is much less sensitive to nonnumerical dimensions that are orthogonal to number (i.e., size and spacing).
source: A recent study, using high-temporal resolution electroencephalography together with a novel stimulus design, demonstrated that early visual cortical activity is uniquely sensitive to the number (abbreviated as N) of a dot array in the absence of any behavioral response, but much less so to nonnumerical dimensions that are orthogonal to number (i.e., size and spacing, abbreviated as Sz and Sp, respectively; see Figure 1A; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2016.

claim: Early cortical sensitivity to numerosity indicates feedforward activity in visual areas V1, V2, and V3.
source: Subsequent behavioral and neural studies showed that this early cortical sensitivity to numerosity indicates feedforward activity in visual areas V1, V2, and V3 (Fornaciai et al., 2017; Fornaciai and Park, 2021; Fornaciai and Park, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fornaciai et al., 2017; Fornaciai and Park, 2021; Fornaciai and Park, 2018.

claim: Numerosity is a basic currency of perceived magnitude early in the visual stream.
source: These results suggest that numerosity is a basic currency of perceived magnitude early in the visual stream.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies.

claim: It is unclear how feedforward neural activity creates a representation of numerosity within early visual brain regions.
source: Nevertheless, it is unclear how feedforward neural activity creates a representation of numerosity within these brain regions.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The view of numerosity as a discrete number of items seems incompatible with the primary modes of information processing in the brain, such as firing rates and population codes, which are continuous.
source: Specifically, the view of numerosity as a discrete number of items seems incompatible with the primary modes of information processing in the brain, such as firing rates and population codes, which are continuous.
evidence: This is a logical observation based on known properties of neural processing.

claim: Some authors assume that continuous nonnumerical magnitude information is encoded first and integrated to produce the representation of numerosity.
source: Indeed, some authors assume that continuous nonnumerical magnitude information is encoded first and integrated to produce the representation of numerosity (Dakin et al., 2011; Gebuis et al., 2016; Leibovich et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dakin et al., 2011; Gebuis et al., 2016; Leibovich et al., 2017.

claim: The magnitude of visual cortical activity is most sensitive to number and is relatively insensitive to other continuous dimensions such as size and spacing of a dot array.
source: In contradiction, however, recent empirical studies demonstrate that the magnitude of visual cortical activity is most sensitive to number and is relatively insensitive to other continuous dimensions such as size and spacing of a dot array (DeWind et al., 2019; Park, 2018; Paul et al., 2022; Van Rinsveld et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DeWind et al., 2019; Park, 2018; Paul et al., 2022; Van Rinsveld et al., 2020.

claim: The Dehaene and Changeux, 1993 model assumes a one-dimensional linear retina.
source: That model (hereafter D&C) assumes a one-dimensional linear retina (each dot is a line segment), and responses are normalized across dot size via a convolution layer that represents combinations of two attributes: (1) dot size, as captured by difference-of-Gaussians contrast filters of different widths; and (2) location, by centering filters at different positions.
evidence: This is a description of the D&C model from the cited paper.

claim: In the Dehaene and Changeux, 1993 model, responses are normalized across dot size via a convolution layer that represents combinations of dot size and location.
source: That model (hereafter D&C) assumes a one-dimensional linear retina (each dot is a line segment), and responses are normalized across dot size via a convolution layer that represents combinations of two attributes: (1) dot size, as captured by difference-of-Gaussians contrast filters of different widths; and (2) location, by centering filters at different positions.
evidence: This is a description of the D&C model from the cited paper.

claim: In the Dehaene and Changeux, 1993 model, the filter that matches the size of each dot dominates the neuronal activity at the location of the dot owing to a winner-take-all lateral inhibition process.
source: In the convolution layer, the filter that matches the size of each dot dominates the neuronal activity at the location of the dot owing to a winner-take-all lateral inhibition process.
evidence: This is a description of the D&C model from the cited paper.

claim: In the Dehaene and Changeux, 1993 model, a summation layer pools the total activity over all the units in the convolution layer to indicate numerosity.
source: To indicate numerosity, a summation layer pools the total activity over all the units in the convolution layer.
evidence: This is a description of the D&C model from the cited paper.

claim: Strong winner-take-all in the convolution layer of the Dehaene and Changeux, 1993 model discretizes visual information, which is implausible for early vision.
source: Of these, the most notable is that strong winner-take-all in the convolution layer discretizes visual information (e.g., discrete locations and discrete sizes yielding a literal count of dots), which is implausible for early vision.
evidence: This is a critique of the D&C model based on knowledge of early vision.

claim: The output of the Dehaene and Changeux, 1993 model is completely insensitive to anything other than number in all situations, which is inconsistent with empirical data.
source: As a result, the output of the model is completely insensitive to anything other than number in all situations, which is inconsistent with empirical data (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a critique of the D&C model supported by a citation to Park et al., 2021.

claim: Stoianov and Zorzi, 2012 developed a hierarchical generative model of the sensory input that demonstrated numerosity-sensitive units after learning to generate its own sensory input.
source: Stoianov and Zorzi, 2012 developed a hierarchical generative model of the sensory input (images of object arrays) and demonstrated that after learning to generate its own sensory input, some units in the hidden layer were sensitive to numerosity irrespective of total area while other units were sensitive to total area irrespective of numerosity.
evidence: This is a description of the Stoianov and Zorzi, 2012 model from the cited paper.

claim: The first hidden layer of the Stoianov and Zorzi, 2012 model developed center-surround representations of different sizes.
source: For example, the first hidden layer developed center-surround representations of different sizes and the second layer developed a pattern of inhibitory connections to units in the first layer that encoded cumulative area.
evidence: This is a description of the Stoianov and Zorzi, 2012 model from the cited paper.

claim: The development of center-surround detectors based on unsupervised learning is a common observation.
source: However, the development of center-surround detectors based on unsupervised learning is a common observation (Bell and Sejnowski, 1997), indicating that such results are not unique to displays of dot arrays, and are instead a natural byproduct of learning in the visual system.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bell and Sejnowski, 1997.

claim: Kim et al., 2021 found that sensitivity and selectivity to numerosity were well captured in a completely untrained convolutional neural network (AlexNet).
source: In a more recent study, Kim et al., 2021 found that sensitivity and selectivity to numerosity were well captured in a completely untrained convolutional neural network (AlexNet) (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), suggesting that a repeated process of convolution and pooling is capable of normalizing continuous dimensions and extracting numerosity information as a statistical regularity of an image.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2021 and Krizhevsky et al., 2012.

claim: A repeated process of convolution and pooling is capable of normalizing continuous dimensions and extracting numerosity information as a statistical regularity of an image.
source: In a more recent study, Kim et al., 2021 found that sensitivity and selectivity to numerosity were well captured in a completely untrained convolutional neural network (AlexNet) (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), suggesting that a repeated process of convolution and pooling is capable of normalizing continuous dimensions and extracting numerosity information as a statistical regularity of an image.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Kim et al., 2021 study.

claim: Center-surround contrast filters at different spatial scales play an important role in numerosity perception.
source: Consistent with prior work, we hypothesize that center-surround contrast filters at different spatial scales play an important role in numerosity perception.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior work.

claim: A moderate level of within-layer normalization is consistent with 'divisive normalization'.
source: In determining the neural mechanisms that are core to numerosity, we note that a moderate level of within-layer normalization is consistent with 'divisive normalization' (Carandini and Heeger, 2011), in which the response of each neuron reflects its driving input divided by the summation of responses from anatomically surrounding neurons (i.e., a normalization pool).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carandini and Heeger, 2011.

claim: In divisive normalization, the response of each neuron reflects its driving input divided by the summation of responses from anatomically surrounding neurons.
source: In determining the neural mechanisms that are core to numerosity, we note that a moderate level of within-layer normalization is consistent with 'divisive normalization' (Carandini and Heeger, 2011), in which the response of each neuron reflects its driving input divided by the summation of responses from anatomically surrounding neurons (i.e., a normalization pool).
evidence: This is a definition of divisive normalization from Carandini and Heeger, 2011.

claim: Divisive normalization is known to exist throughout the cortex, reflecting the shunting inhibition of inhibitory interneurons that limit neural activation within a patch of cortex.
source: Divisive normalization is known to exist throughout the cortex, reflecting the shunting inhibition of inhibitory interneurons that limit neural activation within a patch of cortex (Carandini and Heeger, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carandini and Heeger, 2011.

claim: Divisive normalization is ubiquitous across species and brain systems and hence thought to be a fundamental computation of many neural circuits.
source: A wealth of evidence indicates that divisive normalization is ubiquitous across species and brain systems and hence thought to be a fundamental computation of many neural circuits.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Hierarchically organized multiple center-surround filters of varying size make the network insensitive to spacing.
source: Our results show that (1) hierarchically organized multiple center-surround filters of varying size make the network insensitive to spacing and that (2) divisive normalization implemented across network units makes the network additionally insensitive to size.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Divisive normalization implemented across network units makes the network additionally insensitive to size.
source: Our results show that (1) hierarchically organized multiple center-surround filters of varying size make the network insensitive to spacing and that (2) divisive normalization implemented across network units makes the network additionally insensitive to size.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Divisive normalization occurs over time as well as over space.
source: Divisive normalization not only occurs over space but also over time (Huber and O'Reilly, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huber and O'Reilly, 2003.

claim: Temporal divisive normalization explains the contextual effects of numerosity perception.
source: Thus, we additionally implemented temporal divisive normalization to test if it explains the contextual effects of numerosity perception (Burr and Ross, 2008; Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results and citations to Burr and Ross, 2008; Park et al., 2021.

claim: The summed driving input across all filter sizes is most strongly modulated by both number and size equally but not by spacing.
source: The summed driving input in each filter size showed different effects as a function of number, size, and spacing (Figure 2A), but when the driving input was summed across all filter sizes it was most strongly modulated by both number and size equally but not by spacing (Figure 2B), suggesting that the neural activity tracks total area (TA; see Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The driving input of the convolutional layer primarily captured total pixel intensity of the image regardless of the spatial configuration of dots.
source: In sum, the driving input of the convolutional layer primarily captured total pixel intensity of the image regardless of the spatial configuration of dots.
evidence: This is a summary of the results from the driving input analysis.

claim: Having multiple filter sizes is key to normalizing the spacing dimension.
source: These results illustrate that having multiple filter sizes is key to normalizing the spacing dimension.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Summed normalized responses were strongly modulated by number but much less so by size and spacing.
source: The summed normalized responses, ΣR, were strongly modulated by number but much less so, if any, by size and spacing (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A modest degree of divisive normalization eliminated the effect of size and did not alter the absence of spacing effects.
source: In sum, a modest degree of divisive normalization eliminated the effect of size and, at the same time, did not alter the absence of spacing effects.
evidence: This is a summary of the results from the normalized response analysis.

claim: Irregularly spaced arrays are underestimated compared with regularly spaced arrays.
source: Empirical studies have long shown that irregularly spaced arrays (compared with regularly spaced arrays) and arrays with spatially grouped items (compared with ungrouped items) are all underestimated (Frith and Frit, 1972; Ginsburg, 1976; van Oeffelen and Vos, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Frith and Frit, 1972; Ginsburg, 1976; van Oeffelen and Vos, 1982.

claim: Arrays with spatially grouped items are underestimated compared with ungrouped items.
source: Empirical studies have long shown that irregularly spaced arrays (compared with regularly spaced arrays) and arrays with spatially grouped items (compared with ungrouped items) are all underestimated (Frith and Frit, 1972; Ginsburg, 1976; van Oeffelen and Vos, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Frith and Frit, 1972; Ginsburg, 1976; van Oeffelen and Vos, 1982.

claim: Irregular arrays yielded a 5.98% reduction in normalized response.
source: Irregular arrays yielded a 5.98% reduction (Cohen's d=4.23) and grouped arrays yielded a 2.99% reduction (d=10.02) of normalized response (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Grouped arrays yielded a 2.99% reduction in normalized response.
source: Irregular arrays yielded a 5.98% reduction (Cohen's d=4.23) and grouped arrays yielded a 2.99% reduction (d=10.02) of normalized response (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The underestimation effects in the normalized response can be explained by greater normalization when neurons with overlapping normalization neighborhoods are activated.
source: The underestimation effects in the normalized response can be explained by greater normalization when neurons with overlapping normalization neighborhoods are activated, with this greater overlap occurring in subregions of the images for irregular or grouped dots.
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling results.

claim: The point of subjective equality was about 5.5% lower in dot arrays with heterogeneous sizes compared with dot arrays with homogeneous sizes.
source: A recent behavioral study demonstrated that the point of subjective equality was about 5.5% lower in dot arrays with heterogeneous sizes compared with dot arrays with homogeneous sizes (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2016.

claim: Greater heterogeneity leads to greater underestimation in the model.
source: Consistent with this behavioral phenomenon, our simulations revealed that greater heterogeneity leads to greater underestimation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A moderately heterogeneous array yielded a 1.14% reduction in the magnitude of the normalized response compared to the homogeneous array.
source: As compared to the homogeneous array, a moderately heterogeneous array (labeled 'less heterogeneous') yielded a 1.14% reduction (d=2.43) and the more heterogeneous array yielded a 5.87% reduction (d=8.11) in the magnitude of the normalized response.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results.

claim: The more heterogeneous array yielded a 5.87% reduction in the magnitude of the normalized response compared to the homogeneous array.
source: As compared to the homogeneous array, a moderately heterogeneous array (labeled 'less heterogeneous') yielded a 1.14% reduction (d=2.43) and the more heterogeneous array yielded a 5.87% reduction (d=8.11) in the magnitude of the normalized response.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results.

claim: The summed normalized response of a single dot saturates as dot area increases.
source: This occurs because the summed normalized response of a single dot saturates as dot area increases (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), which interacts with the heterogeneity of the dot array.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Numerosity adaptation reflects divisive normalization across time, similar to adaptation with light or odor.
source: We reasoned that numerosity adaptation might reflect divisive normalization across time, similar to adaptation with light or odor (Carandini and Heeger, 2011), which shifts the response curve and produces a contrast aftereffect.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to Carandini and Heeger, 2011.

claim: The target of 10 dots was underestimated by 28.9% when the adaptor was more numerous than the target.
source: Similar to behavioral results (Aagten-Murphy and Burr, 2016), the target of 10 dots was underestimated by 28.9% (d=18.04) when the adaptor was more numerous than the target and was overestimated by 26.6% (d=14.06) when the adaptor was less numerous than the target.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results and a citation to Aagten-Murphy and Burr, 2016.

claim: The target of 10 dots was overestimated by 26.6% when the adaptor was less numerous than the target.
source: Similar to behavioral results (Aagten-Murphy and Burr, 2016), the target of 10 dots was underestimated by 28.9% (d=18.04) when the adaptor was more numerous than the target and was overestimated by 26.6% (d=14.06) when the adaptor was less numerous than the target.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results and a citation to Aagten-Murphy and Burr, 2016.

claim: The model does not 'know' the number of dots in the adaptor image.
source: It is important to note that the model does not 'know' the number of dots in the adaptor image.
evidence: This is a clarification about how the model works.

claim: No adaptation effect emerges for size or spacing variables in the model.
source: Indeed, because the normalized response is less sensitive to variation in size or spacing, no adaptation effect emerges for those variables (Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The effect of size is negligible in the context of a trial sequence that varies size, spacing, and number.
source: Studies show that the effect of size is negligible in the context of a trial sequence that varies size, spacing, and number (Park et al., 2016), but that the effect of size becomes apparent when number and spacing are held constant while varying only size (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2016 and Park et al., 2021.

claim: The effect of size becomes apparent when number and spacing are held constant while varying only size.
source: Studies show that the effect of size is negligible in the context of a trial sequence that varies size, spacing, and number (Park et al., 2016), but that the effect of size becomes apparent when number and spacing are held constant while varying only size (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2016 and Park et al., 2021.

claim: In the context where all dimensions varied, the three levels of Sz had no linear association with M*.
source: In the context where all dimensions varied, the three levels of Sz had no linear association with M*; the 95th percentile confidence interval of the ordinary-least-square linear slope of M* as a function of Sz was [–0.0243, 0.0182], which includes 0.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results.

claim: In the context where only size varied, M* was positively correlated with Sz.
source: In contrast, in the context where only size varied, M* was positively correlated with Sz; slope confidence interval of [0.00315, 0.00359], which excludes 0.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results.

claim: The implementation of hierarchically organized multiple sizes of center-surround filters effectively normalizes spacing owing to offsetting factors.
source: First, the implementation of hierarchically organized multiple sizes of center-surround filters effectively normalizes spacing owing to offsetting factors (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The implementation of divisive normalization reduces the effect of size by reducing activity at larger filter sizes that have overlapping normalization neighborhoods.
source: Second, the implementation of divisive normalization reduces the effect of size by reducing activity at larger filter sizes that have overlapping normalization neighborhoods (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: Divisive normalization is a within-layer effect, reflecting recurrent inhibition between center-surround filters owing to inhibitory interneurons.
source: Critically, divisive normalization is a within-layer effect, reflecting recurrent inhibition between center-surround filters owing to inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of divisive normalization.

claim: Contrast filters at different spatial scales and divisive normalization naturally increases sensitivity to the number of items in a visual scene.
source: In sum, contrast filters at different spatial scales and divisive normalization naturally increases sensitivity to the number of items in a visual scene.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Because these neurocomputational principles are commonly found in visual animals, visual perception of numerosity is a natural, emergent phenomenon.
source: Because these neurocomputational principles are commonly found in visual animals, this suggests that visual perception of numerosity is a natural, emergent phenomenon.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results and knowledge of visual systems.

claim: The summed normalized output of the neuronal activity is sensitive to numerosity but shows little variation with size and spacing.
source: A key result from the current model is that the summed normalized output of the neuronal activity is sensitive to numerosity but shows little variation with size and spacing.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results.

claim: This pattern is consistent with neural studies finding similar results for the summed response of V1, V2, and V3 in the absence of any behavioral judgment.
source: This pattern is consistent with neural studies finding similar results for the summed response of V1, V2, and V3 in the absence of any behavioral judgment (Fornaciai et al., 2017; Fornaciai and Park, 2018; Paul et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fornaciai et al., 2017; Fornaciai and Park, 2018; Paul et al., 2022.

claim: The abundance of simulated neurons sensitive to nonnumerical dimensions in deep neural network models is inconsistent with population-level neural activity in early visual cortex.
source: Although the few units that were sensitive to numerosity could explain behavior, the abundance of simulated neurons sensitive to nonnumerical dimensions is inconsistent with population-level neural activity, which fails to show sensitivity to these nonnumerical dimensions in early visual cortex (DeWind et al., 2019; Park, 2018; Van Rinsveld et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DeWind et al., 2019; Park, 2018; Van Rinsveld et al., 2020.

claim: A key difference between the current model and previous computational models is the inclusion of divisive normalization in the center-surround convolution layer.
source: A key difference between the current model and previous computational models is the inclusion of divisive normalization in the center-surround convolution layer.
evidence: This is a statement about the model design.

claim: The D&C model is one-dimensional, simulating a linear retina, whereas the current model simulates a two-dimensional retina feeding into center-surround filters.
source: First, the D&C model is one-dimensional, simulating a linear retina, whereas we model a two-dimensional retina feeding into center-surround filters, allowing application to the two-dimensional images used in numerosity experiments (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current model and the D&C model.

claim: Extreme winner-take-all normalization in the convolution layer of the D&C model implausibly limits visual precision by discretizing the visual response.
source: Second, extreme winner-take-all normalization in the convolution layer of the D&C model implausibly limits visual precision by discretizing the visual response.
evidence: This is a critique of the D&C model.

claim: By using divisive normalization in the current model, each dot produces activity at many locations and many filter sizes despite normalization.
source: In contrast, by using divisive normalization in the current model, each dot produces activity at many locations and many filter sizes despite normalization, and a population could be used to determine exact location and size.
evidence: This is a description of how the current model differs from the D&C model.

claim: Extreme winner-take-all normalization in the D&C model eliminates all information other than dot size and location.
source: Third, extreme winner-take-all normalization also eliminates all information other than dot size and location.
evidence: This is a critique of the D&C model.

claim: By using divisive normalization, the current model represents other attributes such as edges and groupings of dots.
source: By using divisive normalization, the current model represents other attributes such as edges and groupings of dots (Figure 1B) and these other attributes provide a different explanation of numerosity sensitivity as compared to D&C.
evidence: This is a description of how the current model differs from the D&C model.

claim: The D&C model does not include temporal normalization.
source: The final difference is that the D&C model does not include temporal normalization, which we show to be critical for explaining adaptation and context effects.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current model and the D&C model.

claim: Neural activity in V1 increases monotonically with numerosity.
source: Finally, a recent fMRI study reported that neural activity in V1 increases monotonically with numerosity (Paul et al., 2022), which is consistent with the current model at a surface level.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Paul et al., 2022.

claim: Paul et al., 2022 concluded that the monotonic increase in V1 activity was better explained by aggregate Fourier power than by numerosity.
source: The authors, however, concluded that this monotonic increase was better explained by aggregate Fourier power than by numerosity.
evidence: This is a description of the conclusions from Paul et al., 2022.

claim: Fourier power uses spatially unbounded sine waves that have little biological plausibility.
source: First, Fourier power uses spatially unbounded sine waves that have little biological plausibility (unlike center-surround or Gabor filters, which are spatially limited).
evidence: This is a critique of the Fourier power explanation based on knowledge of biological plausibility.

claim: The aggregate Fourier power metric used by Paul et al., 2022 aggregated only up through the first (or an nth) harmonic, but the value of the harmonic on the frequency spectrum is dictated by dot size and dot groupings.
source: Second, more critically, the aggregate Fourier power metric used by Paul et al., 2022 aggregated only up through the first (or an nth) harmonic, but the value of the harmonic on the frequency spectrum is dictated by dot size and dot groupings.
evidence: This is a critique of the Fourier power explanation from Paul et al., 2022.

claim: It is unclear how the visual system could know in advance an appropriate cutoff for a harmonic in the Fourier power metric.
source: In other words, the Fourier metric required a priori knowledge about each image, and it is unclear how the visual system could know in advance an appropriate cutoff for a harmonic.
evidence: This is a critique of the Fourier power explanation.

claim: Specific quantitative predictions will change depending on specific model assumptions.
source: However, specific quantitative predictions will change depending on specific model assumptions.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the model.

claim: When dots are presented in the periphery where RF sizes are larger, numerosity perception exhibits different behavioral characteristics.
source: For instance, studies found that when dots are presented in the periphery where RF sizes are larger (Li et al., 2021; Valsecchi et al., 2013) or if the dots are crowded and hard to individuate (Anobile et al., 2014), numerosity perception exhibits different behavioral characteristics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2021; Valsecchi et al., 2013; Anobile et al., 2014.

claim: When dots are crowded and hard to individuate, numerosity perception exhibits different behavioral characteristics.
source: For instance, studies found that when dots are presented in the periphery where RF sizes are larger (Li et al., 2021; Valsecchi et al., 2013) or if the dots are crowded and hard to individuate (Anobile et al., 2014), numerosity perception exhibits different behavioral characteristics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2021; Valsecchi et al., 2013; Anobile et al., 2014.

claim: For very small dots densely packed in a circular aperture, the summation of normalized responses was still primarily sensitive to number, but that sensitivity was smaller compared to the original simulation.
source: We simulated one extreme by submitting to the model images that contained very small dots (too small to allow edge responses) densely packed in a circular aperture. For this extreme, the summation of normalized responses was still primarily sensitive to number, but that sensitivity was smaller compared to our original simulation, and there was also some moderate sensitivity to size and spacing (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The success of this model does not necessarily imply that neuronal responses in early visual regions directly determine behavioral responses.
source: The success of this model does not necessarily imply that neuronal responses in early visual regions directly determine behavioral responses (see Fornaciai and Park, 2018).
evidence: This is a clarification about the interpretation of the model results, supported by a citation to Fornaciai and Park, 2018.

claim: Normalized response magnitude in early visual regions may be the basic currency from which numerosity judgments are made.
source: Instead, these results, together with previous electrophysiology results, suggest that normalized response magnitude in early visual regions may be the basic currency from which numerosity judgments are made.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results and previous electrophysiology results.

claim: If decisional uncertainty is modeled by assuming a constant level of decisional noise, the model will naturally produce Weber's scaling law of just noticeable differences.
source: For instance, if decisional uncertainty is modeled by assuming a constant level of decisional noise, regardless of the visual information, then the model will naturally produce Weber's scaling law of just noticeable differences considering that the normalized response follows a log-linear pattern as a function of numerosity (see Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a speculation about how the model could be extended to explain behavioral phenomena.

claim: The connectedness illusion involves an array with dots connected pairwise with thin lines being underestimated (by up to 20%) compared to the same array without the lines connected.
source: For example, another well-known visual illusion is the effect of connectedness, whereby an array with dots connected pairwise with thin lines is underestimated (by up to 20%) compared to the same array without the lines connected (Franconeri et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Franconeri et al., 2009.

claim: A small magnitude (6%) connectedness illusion emerges with center-surround filters.
source: Nonetheless, a small magnitude (6%) connectedness illusion emerges with center-surround filters (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Divisive normalization in a single convolutional layer with hierarchically organized center-surround filters naturally enhances sensitivity to the discrete number of items in a visual scene by reducing the effects of size and spacing.
source: In conclusion, our results indicate that divisive normalization in a single convolutional layer with hierarchically organized center-surround filters naturally enhances sensitivity to the discrete number of items in a visual scene by reducing the effects of size and spacing, consistent with recent empirical studies demonstrating direct and rapid encoding of numerosity (Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the modeling results, supported by a citation to Park et al., 2016.

claim: Various well-known numerosity illusions across space and time arise naturally within the same neural responses that encode numerosity, rather than reflecting later stage processes.
source: This account predicts that various well-known numerosity illusions across space and time arise naturally within the same neural responses that encode numerosity, rather than reflecting later stage processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.
